outline.chapter_title: Procedural Posture and Standards of Review
outline.description: This chapter establishes the foundational context of the litigation, including the parties involved, the patents at issue, the jury's initial verdict, and the specific legal standards the Federal Circuit applies when reviewing a denial of Judgment as a Matter of Law (JMOL) and a motion for a new trial.
subtopics: Overview of the '134 and '775 Patents regarding Intermodulation Product (IMP) interference
The District Court proceedings: Jury findings of validity, infringement, and damages award
Standard of Review for JMOL under Fifth Circuit law: De novo review and the 'overwhelming evidence' threshold
Standard of Review for infringement findings: The 'substantial evidence' test

outline.chapter_title: Infringement Analysis of the '134 Patent: The Sampling Limitation
outline.description: This chapter dissect the court's reasoning regarding Claim 1 of the '134 patent, focusing on the critical failure of Finesse's expert to map the accused product's signals to the claim limitation requiring the sampling of both 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals' simultaneously.
subtopics: Claim Construction: The requirement to sample a passband containing both signal types before processing
The Expert's Initial Mapping: Identifying the 'modeled PIM path' as the 'interference generating signal'
The Logical Impossibility: Why a modeled signal generated post-sampling cannot be sampled by the RF ADC
Analysis of Contradictory Testimony: The shift from 'modeled PIM path' to undefined inputs 'x1 and x2'
Legal Principle: Insufficiency of self-contradictory expert testimony to support a jury verdict

outline.chapter_title: Infringement Analysis of the '775 Patent: Signal Count and Multiplication Steps
outline.description: This chapter examines the dispute over the '775 patent, specifically addressing whether using two unique inputs satisfies the 'three signals' limitation and why the evidence failed to prove the performance of the seven specific mathematical multiplications required by the claims.
subtopics: Claim Construction Debate: Whether 'three signals' requires three unique inputs or merely three separately identifiable instances
Prosecution History Estoppel: Why amending claims to specify 'three signals' did not surrender coverage for devices using two unique inputs
The Mathematical Gap: Comparing the claimed seven third-order multiplications against the accused product's three distinct operations
Flaws in Expert Mapping: The discrepancy between claimed variables (S1, S2, S3) and accused operations involving modulus and complex conjugates
The Prohibition on Post-Hoc Rationalization: Why arguments raised only on appeal cannot cure evidentiary gaps at trial

outline.description: This final chapter outlines the appellate court's ultimate ruling reversing the infringement findings and explains the automatic consequence of that reversal on previously awarded damages, rendering a separate analysis of the damages calculation unnecessary.
subtopics: Summary of Holdings: Reversal of JMOL denials for both patents due to lack of substantial evidence
The Nexus Between Liability and Remedies: Why vacating infringement necessitates vacating damages
Procedural Outcome: Remand implications and allocation of costs to Appellants
